clue.text: South-east Asians, dreadful maniacs imprisoning person

indicators.note: imprisoning means the shuffled letters lock another piece up inside them
dreadful suggests the maniacs are in a terrible state, so their letters are jumbled

parts.note: BOD is informal British slang for a person, as in 'odd bod'

explanation.surface: Travellers from South-east Asia are held captive by a gang of terrible lunatics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dreadful' reads as describing the maniacs but is the anagram signal; 'imprisoning' sets the person inside the jumbled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: People from Cambodia are natives of a country in South-east Asia, so they are South-east Asians.

clue.text: Sack that's left inside bar

indicators.note: inside places one piece within the other, here the letter for left

parts.note: to sack someone is to give them the axe

explanation.surface: A bag left behind in a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: An axle is the rod or bar on which a wheel turns.

clue.text: That is buried in plot further away

indicators.note: is buried in places the word for that within the word for plot, like a body in the ground

parts.note: a plot of garden ground is a bed
yon is an old or dialect word for that, as in 'yon hill'

explanation.surface: Something lies buried in a garden plot farther off.
explanation.definitionFit: Beyond means further away, on the far side of something.

clue.text: Place in Surrey could be complete with two sovereigns

parts.note: to do a job is to complete it
R stands for Rex, the Latin for king, one sovereign
a king is the second sovereign

explanation.surface: A Surrey town might be fully equipped with a pair of gold coins.
explanation.walkthrough: A sovereign is also an old British gold coin, which is the surface's picture. DORKING is a market town in Surrey, a county south of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorking is a town in the English county of Surrey, so it is a place there.

clue.text: Chemical in a shapeless mass not soft

indicators.note: not soft drops P, the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning soft

parts.note: a lump is a shapeless mass

explanation.surface: A chemical found in a soft, formless blob.
explanation.walkthrough: In music P (piano) means soft, so 'not soft' drops that letter from the shapeless mass.
explanation.definitionFit: Alum is a chemical compound, a double sulphate used in dyeing and tanning.

clue.text: A horse may be second — rotten

parts.note: an addled egg is a rotten one

explanation.surface: A horse might come second, which is a rotten result.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse is saddled when it has a saddle put on it ready for riding, so a horse may be in that state.

clue.text: Clones are, come what may

definitions.meaning: clones are identical copies of one another, every one alike
an idiom meaning regardless, whatever happens

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both identical in every case and nevertheless, regardless of circumstances.

clue.text: Dejected, being deprived of whisky?

definitions.meaning: whisky is a spirit, so having none of it is a playful sense

explanation.definitionFit: Lifeless and without vigour is the usual sense; the second plays on spirits as strong drink.

clue.text: Friends about to produce a hit

indicators.note: about signals turning round, so the word for friends reads backwards

parts.note: pals are friends

explanation.surface: Mates are on the point of throwing a punch.
explanation.definitionFit: A slap is a blow with the open hand, so it counts as a hit.

clue.text: In which someone may be out of his or her class?

definitions.text: In which someone may be out of his or her class?

parts.words: In which someone may be out of his or her class?
parts.note: out of class sounds like being socially out of place, but means a pupil out of the classroom at break time

explanation.definitionFit: A school yard where children play at break, when they are outside lessons.

clue.text: German boy certainly not a Bunter type

definitions.meaning: Billy Bunter is the greedy fat schoolboy of British children's stories, the opposite of someone cutting down on food

explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is a famously greedy, overweight schoolboy from Frank Richards' British school stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Dieter is a German first name, and a person on a diet is anything but a glutton like Bunter.

clue.text: What may give cover to one who is lying

definitions.text: What may give cover to one who is lying

parts.words: What may give cover to one who is lying
parts.note: cover for a liar suggests an alibi, but the one lying is lying down in bed under sheets and blankets

explanation.definitionFit: Sheets, blankets and quilts cover a sleeper lying in bed.

clue.text: A soberness not usually found in ladies

indicators.note: not usually suggests an unusual arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Sober restraint is rarely seen among women of rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not usually' shuffles A SOBERNESS into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Baronesses are titled women, peeresses addressed as Lady, hence ladies.

clue.text: Damage makes building material fade badly on top

indicators.note: on top places the shuffled letters above the next piece in this down entry
badly signals the word fade being mangled into a new order

parts.note: cement is a building material

explanation.surface: Damage causes building materials to fade badly from the top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' scrambles fade, and 'on top' sets it above the building material in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Defacement is damage spoiling the surface or appearance of something.

clue.text: Sort of very clever chap? Not I

indicators.note: Not means the following letter is left out of the word for a clever chap

parts.note: a genius is a very clever person

explanation.surface: Which kind of brilliant man is it? Not me.
explanation.definitionFit: A genus is a kind or class, as in a sort of thing.

clue.text: Senior schoolgirl gets a bit twisted, becoming model

indicators.note: a bit twisted means a small part of the word is shifted out of place

parts.note: a prefect is a senior pupil with authority in a British school

explanation.surface: A head girl goes slightly off the rails and becomes a role model.
explanation.walkthrough: In a British school a PREFECT is a senior pupil given duties. Moving its R one place along gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Perfect describes an ideal example, as a model pupil is.

clue.text: Drinks — any number needed in the mines

indicators.note: needed in places the letter for a number inside the word for mines

parts.note: pits are coal mines
N stands for any number in algebra

explanation.surface: Any number of beers are needed down in the mines.
explanation.definitionFit: A pint is a measure of beer, so pints are drinks.

clue.text: Frigid upper-class girl with little money once

parts.note: gel is a girl as pronounced in a posh accent
1d was one old penny in British coinage, a small sum before decimalisation

explanation.surface: A frosty posh girl with only a penny to her name in the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 British money was written in pounds, shillings and pence, with d for penny; 1d, written ID, was one penny.
explanation.definitionFit: Gelid means icy cold, a close synonym of frigid.

clue.text: Split wood brought back and lit finally

indicators.note: brought back means the word for wood is turned round

parts.note: fir is a wood

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of the word lit

explanation.surface: Wood is split, carried home and finally set alight.
explanation.definitionFit: A rift is a split or crack, also a break in a relationship.

clue.text: Mist somewhere in Middlesex, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the place name is said out loud for its sound

parts.note: Hayes is a town in the old county of Middlesex, west of London

explanation.surface: Fog in a Middlesex town, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: Middlesex is a former county now largely part of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Haze is a light mist or obscuring vapour in the air.

clue.text: Leave old city in South America

parts.note: to quit is to leave

explanation.surface: Departing from an ancient South American city.
explanation.definitionFit: Quito is the capital city of Ecuador in South America.

clue.text: The tiniest bit gives a fashion designer hesitation

parts.note: Mary Quant was a British fashion designer famed for the miniskirt
um is a sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A designer hesitates over the smallest detail.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary Quant was the British designer associated with 1960s London fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: In physics a quantum is the smallest discrete amount of something, the tiniest bit.

clue.text: Books packaged together in vehicle

definitions.meaning: a single volume collecting several works
the old full name of a bus

explanation.definitionFit: An omnibus is both a collected edition of books and the original word for a bus.

clue.text: Core group of students tackling tricky clue

indicators.note: tackling suggests gripping something, so one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: NUS is the National Union of Students in Britain

indicators.note: tricky signals that the letters of clue are awkwardly rearranged

explanation.surface: A core group of students tackle a tricky crossword clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The NUS is Britain's National Union of Students; 'tricky' scrambles clue, and 'tackling' sets it inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A nucleus is the central core of something, as of an atom or cell.

clue.text: Hoarding pounds, misers unlikely to be such?

definitions.text: Hoarding pounds, misers unlikely to be such?

indicators.note: hoarding means the word misers keeps another letter stored inside it
unlikely signals that the letters must be reordered into an unexpected arrangement

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Stingy people who stockpile money are rarely the cheerful sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hoarding' puts L into MISERS, and 'unlikely' rearranges the lot. The whole clue also says misers seldom grin.
explanation.definitionFit: Smilers are people who smile, which a grasping miser is not known for doing.

clue.text: Desire shown by one bather, primarily to get into pool

indicators.note: to get into puts the letters inside the word for a pool

parts.note: a lido is a public open-air swimming pool
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: primarily takes the first letter of the word bather

explanation.surface: Someone shows an urge to jump into the pool for a swim.
explanation.definitionFit: Libido is sexual desire or drive.

clue.text: Judge a script brought in by boy

indicators.note: brought in by places the pieces inside the word for boy

parts.note: a son is a boy
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript, a written script

explanation.surface: A screenplay delivered by a lad to a judge.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Bible, Samson was one of the Judges of Israel.
explanation.definitionFit: Samson is one of the Judges of Israel in the Old Testament book of Judges.

clue.text: Criticism when one gets cut shaving?

indicators.note: gets cut means the word loses its tail, its last letter chopped off

parts.note: a shaving is a thin flake cut from something

explanation.surface: What you hear when someone nicks himself while shaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets cut' removes the final E from FLAKE.
explanation.definitionFit: Flak is strong adverse criticism, from anti-aircraft fire.

clue.text: Contend that's not right, making complaint

indicators.note: that's not says the following letter is absent from the word for contend

parts.note: to argue is to contend

explanation.surface: Arguing that something is wrong, one lodges a complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Ague is a feverish illness, and an illness is a complaint in the medical sense.

clue.text: One who has lost all his cash simply can't get over it!

definitions.text: One who has lost all his cash simply can't get over it!

parts.words: One who has lost all his cash simply can't get over it!
parts.note: cannot get over it sounds like enduring grief, but means literally unable to cross a structure that charges a fee

explanation.definitionFit: A bridge where a charge must be paid to cross, impossible for a penniless traveller.

clue.text: Bird's merit being expressed audibly

indicators.note: expressed audibly signals that the word is spoken, giving its sound

parts.note: to merit something is to earn it

explanation.surface: A bird's worth is made known out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is a sea eagle, a bird often met in crosswords.

clue.text: Works at Llantrisant maybe and shows a profit

definitions.meaning: the Royal Mint is at Llantrisant in Wales, where coins are produced

explanation.walkthrough: Llantrisant in south Wales is home to the Royal Mint, which produces Britain's coins.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally minting coins, and idiomatically being profitable.
